Early bar zithers were widely used in sub-Saharan Africa, especially in West and Central Africa, where local peoples regard them as an important part of traditional musical culture. Over time the bar zither developed many forms, and players used the voice, gourds or animal bladders as natural resonators to strengthen the sound. In the course of this development different regions created variants with local character, according to local resources and taste. From the nineteenth century, with the rise of ethnomusicology, Western scholars took a strong interest in the bar zither, which spread knowledge and study of the instrument worldwide. The establishment of the Hornbostel–Sachs classification gave it a scientific framework and made it an important object of comparative musicology, and it gained new life in the global folk music revival.
